title: Single-row edging
subtitle: How to add a clean, simple border along any crochet edge in one pass
excerpt: A single-row edging in double crochet is the most useful finishing technique in crochet. It stabilises the edge, adds a professional finish, and serves as the base for any decorative border added later.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The side edges of a flat crocheted piece, formed by the turning chains and the first or last stitch of each row.
The face of the fabric that is intended to show. In flat crochet, the right side faces you on odd-numbered rows if working with the right side facing.

content.text: A single-row edging adds one pass of double crochet around the entire outer edge of a piece. It covers the raw

edges, straightens any irregular row ends, and provides a clean loop into which a second decorative border can be worked later. It is the standard first step before adding crab stitch, scallops, or any other finishing border.
facing you. Join with a slip stitch at any corner or at the first stitch of a top or bottom edge. Chain 1. The chain 1 does not count as a stitch.
Top or bottom edge (the last or first row): work 1 double crochet into each stitch across. One stitch per stitch.
Side edges (selvedge): work stitches evenly into the end of each row. A rough guide is 1 double crochet per double crochet row, or 2 double crochets per treble row. Adjust to keep the edge flat.
Corners: work 3 stitches into each corner stitch to allow the border to turn without pulling.
Continue around all four sides, keeping the stitch count even on opposite edges.
When back at the start, join with a slip stitch to the top of the first double crochet.
If the edging will stay as a single row, fasten off. If a second border follows, proceed without fastening off.

items.symptom: The side edges ripple or ruffle
items.cause: Too many stitches were worked along the selvedge relative to the row height.
items.fix: Reduce to 1 double crochet per row on the side edges, or use a slip stitch between every second row. Pull the edge flat and count; if it waves, there are too many stitches.

items.cause: Too few stitches were worked into the selvedge.
items.fix: Add one stitch every third or fourth row along the selvedge until the edge lies flat.

items.symptom: The corners do not lie flat and pull tight
items.cause: Fewer than 3 stitches were worked into the corner stitch.
items.fix: Work 3 double crochets into the corner stitch. On square corners with thick yarn, 5 stitches may be needed.

content.text: Once a flat single-row edging is reliable, add a second round in a contrasting colour for a stripe effect, or switch to crab stitch on the second round for a corded edge. Both are worked directly on top of the single-row base.
